title: Battle of Blue Licks
summary: On August 19, 1782, a British and Native force ambushed about 180 Kentucky militia at the Lower Blue Licks, the largest Revolutionary War battle fought in Kentucky.
bodyMarkdown:
On the morning of August 19, 1782, about 180 mounted Kentucky militiamen reached a bend of the [Licking River](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/590) at the [Lower Blue Licks](/#map/stories/battle-of-blue-licks), a salt spring that buffalo had worn bare. Across the ford, a few warriors walked over a rocky ridge and out of sight. Within about fifteen minutes the militia had been routed, and some 60 to 77 of them were dead.

The battle took place ten months after Yorktown. It was the largest Revolutionary War battle fought in Kentucky, and many Kentuckians still call it the war's last battle ([American Battlefield Trust](https://www.battlefields.org/learn/revolutionary-war/battles/blue-licks)).

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Date** | August 19, 1782 ⚑ (Caldwell's report dates it August 18)¹ |
| **Place** | Lower Blue Licks, Licking River, Robertson County. [See on the map](/#map/stories/battle-of-blue-licks) |
| **War** | American Revolution, western theater |
| **Commanders** | Kentucky militia: [John Todd](/people/#john-todd), [Stephen Trigg](/people/#stephen-trigg), [Daniel Boone](/people/#daniel-boone), [Hugh McGary](/people/#hugh-mcgary). British and Native force: [William Caldwell](/people/#william-caldwell), with Indian Department officers [Alexander McKee](/people/#alexander-mckee) and [Simon Girty](/people/#simon-girty) |
| **Forces** | Militia: about 176–182. British and Native force: about 200–300 Rangers and warriors ⚑² |
| **Losses** | Militia: about 60–77 killed and about 7–12 captured ⚑. British and Native force: about 7–11 killed and 10–14 wounded ⚑² |
| **Result** | British and Native victory; the Kentucky militia was routed |

## Goals of each side

### The Native nations

Most of the warriors were [Wyandot](/stories/wyandot-on-kentuckys-northern-frontier/), along with men from the Great Lakes ("Lake") nations. Their commander wrote that the Wyandots supplied his food ([Caldwell, 1782](https://www.royalprovincial.com/history/battles/brcald1.shtml)). Kentucky sources also name Shawnee and Delaware (Lenape) warriors ([ExploreKYHistory](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/590)).

For the Shawnee and their neighbors, Kentucky was a hunting ground their own leaders had never agreed to give up. It had been signed away by others in the [Treaty of Fort Stanwix (1768)](/stories/treaty-of-fort-stanwix-1768/), and Shawnee leaders had yielded it under pressure at [Camp Charlotte (1774)](/stories/treaty-of-camp-charlotte-1774/). Settler stations and Kentucky expeditions north of the Ohio threatened their towns and food supply.

The spring of 1782 had hardened feelings. In March, Pennsylvania militia killed some 90 Christian Lenape who had surrendered their arms at the Moravian mission of [Gnadenhutten](https://www.battlefields.org/learn/revolutionary-war/battles/gnadenhutten), among them the Delaware elder [Glikhikan](https://www.biographi.ca/en/bio/glikhikan_4E.html) ([DCB, Girty](https://www.biographi.ca/en/bio/girty_simon_5E.html)). American Battlefield Trust writes that the massacre fed a desire for revenge in the Sandusky towns. No source ties it directly to Blue Licks.

### The British at Detroit

Britain ran its western war from Detroit through the Indian Department, which supplied and advised allied nations. Its aim was to keep the Americans busy on the frontier and away from Detroit, which had been threatened since [George Rogers Clark](/stories/george-rogers-clark/) took Vincennes in 1779 ([DCB, Caldwell](https://www.biographi.ca/en/bio/caldwell_william_1822_6E.html)).

Capt. **William Caldwell** was an Irish-born Loyalist officer in Butler's Rangers, called "a very active Partisan" by his commandant. In June 1782 his force had defeated Col. William Crawford's expedition on the upper Sandusky ([DCB, Caldwell](https://www.biographi.ca/en/bio/caldwell_william_1822_6E.html)).

**Alexander McKee**, a captain and interpreter with "extensive influence among the Indians," joined the attack on Bryan's Station ([DCB, McKee](https://www.biographi.ca/en/bio/mckee_alexander_4E.html)). **Simon Girty** had been captured as a boy and raised among the Senecas. In 1778 he left the Americans to interpret for the British. The DCB warns that a "white savage" legend grew out of "distortions of fact" ([DCB, Girty](https://www.biographi.ca/en/bio/girty_simon_5E.html); see [our Girty story](/stories/simon-girty-interpreter-at-bryan-station-1782/)). ⚑ His brothers James and George also served the Indian Department, but no source we have places either one at Blue Licks.

### The Kentucky militia

The stations had just been attacked, and their cattle, hogs and crops had been destroyed ([Caldwell, 1782](https://www.royalprovincial.com/history/battles/brcald1.shtml)). The militia's expected answer was to pursue the raiders before they crossed the Ohio.

**Col. [John Todd](/stories/col-john-todd-of-lexington/)** of Fayette County was the senior officer. **Lt. Col. [Stephen Trigg](/stories/col-stephen-trigg-of-viney-grove/)** led the Lincoln County men, with **Maj. [Hugh McGary](/stories/hugh-mcgary-the-blue-licks-hothead/)**. **Lt. Col. Daniel Boone** commanded the Fayette left ([Boone to Harrison, 1782](https://kynghistory.ky.gov/Our-History/History-of-the-Guard/Pages/The-Battle-of-Blue-Licks.aspx)). Col. [Benjamin Logan](/stories/benjamin-logan/) was raising more Lincoln men and had not yet arrived.

## Lead-up

In early August, Caldwell had gathered what he called "Eleven hundred Indians." A false report that Clark was marching on the Shawnee towns broke the gathering up. Caldwell then crossed the Ohio "with three Hundred Indians and Rangers" ([Caldwell, 1782](https://www.royalprovincial.com/history/battles/brcald1.shtml)).

They surrounded [Bryan's Station](/stories/bryan-station-siege-august-1782/) near Lexington. They burned outbuildings and killed livestock, but they could not take the fort. They withdrew on the morning of August 17. Caldwell chose the Blue Licks road because the ground there was "more advantageous in case the Enemy should pursue."

## Battle timeline

- **Aug. 15–16, 1782**: Caldwell's force surrounds Bryan's Station. ⚑ Caldwell gives the 15th; Boone and [Levi Todd](/stories/levi-todd-lexington-co-founder/) give the 16th.¹
- **Aug. 17**: The attackers withdraw and camp at the Blue Licks.
- **Aug. 18**: About 176–182 militia ride out from Bryan's Station on the trail, roughly 40 miles ([Filson, 1784](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/909/909-h/909-h.htm)).
- **Aug. 19, morning**: At the ford the officers confer. Boone urges caution because of the ravines ahead ([ExploreKYHistory](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/590)).
- **Aug. 19**: The militia cross and form three divisions: Trigg on the right, Todd and McGary in the center, Boone on the left, and Maj. [Silas Harlan](/stories/maj-silas-harlan/) leading the advance.
- **Aug. 19**: They close "within about forty yards" before the firing starts. Boone's wing pushes forward, but the right breaks "at the first fire" and warriors get into the rear ([Boone to Harrison](https://kynghistory.ky.gov/Our-History/History-of-the-Guard/Pages/The-Battle-of-Blue-Licks.aspx)).
- **Aug. 19**: Todd, Trigg, Harlan and Boone's son [Israel](/people/#israel-boone) are killed. The militia break back across the river, fighting hand to hand.
- **Aug. 19–20**: The survivors meet Logan's relief column.
- **About Aug. 24**: Logan's force of about 460 returns and buries the dead. Boone wrote: "We found forty-three on the ground."

⚑ **The McGary tradition.** A widely told story says McGary spurred into the ford shouting, "Them that ain't cowards follow me." It comes from recollections gathered decades later and retold in histories such as [HistoryNet's account](https://historynet.com/battle-of-blue-licks/). Neither Boone's 1782 letter nor his 1784 narrative mentions it. ExploreKYHistory says only that the Kentuckians "ignored Boone's advice."

## People involved

- [John Todd](/people/#john-todd), militia: commanding officer; killed.
- [Stephen Trigg](/people/#stephen-trigg), militia: right wing; killed.
- [Daniel Boone](/people/#daniel-boone), militia: left wing; survived.
- [Israel Boone](/people/#israel-boone), militia: Boone's son; killed.
- [Hugh McGary](/people/#hugh-mcgary), militia: center; survived.
- [Silas Harlan](/people/#silas-harlan), militia: advance party; killed.
- [Robert Patterson](/people/#robert-patterson), militia: captain; survived ([monument roll](https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=285554)).
- [Levi Todd](/people/#levi-todd), militia: major; helped bury the dead.
- [Benjamin Logan](/people/#benjamin-logan), militia: relief column.
- [William Caldwell](/people/#william-caldwell), British: commander.
- [Alexander McKee](/people/#alexander-mckee), Indian Department.
- [Simon Girty](/people/#simon-girty), Indian Department interpreter.
- Wyandot, Shawnee, Lenape and Lake nations leaders: their names are not recorded in the sources we have.

## Location

The ridge and ford lie inside Blue Licks Battlefield State Resort Park on US 68, where [KHS marker #18](https://history.ky.gov/markers/blue-licks-battlefield) stands. Visitors can walk to the monument and the mass grave on the ridge Caldwell held ([American Battlefield Trust](https://www.battlefields.org/learn/revolutionary-war/battles/blue-licks)). [See it on the map](/#map/stories/battle-of-blue-licks).

## Outcome and why it mattered

Caldwell reported one Ranger and six warriors killed and ten wounded. He claimed his force had "killed and took One hundred and Forty six," a figure that wrongly counted Boone and McGary among the dead ([Caldwell, 1782](https://www.royalprovincial.com/history/battles/brcald1.shtml)). ⚑ Kentucky dead range from 60 in Filson's book to 77 in Boone's letter.

For Kentucky it was a crippling loss of leaders. On August 30 Boone asked Virginia's governor for 500 men: "are we to be wholly forgotten?" For the Native nations it was a clear victory, but in November Clark led Kentucky militia against the Shawnee towns on the Great Miami. The inhabitants left, and five towns and their corn were burned ([Filson, 1784](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/909/909-h/909-h.htm)).

Caldwell's Rangers came home "hardly capable of taking the field again," and the war moved to the peace table ([DCB](https://www.biographi.ca/en/bio/caldwell_william_1822_6E.html)). The [Treaty of Paris](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1776-1783/treaty) gave the land to the United States without consulting the Native nations, which set up a dozen more years of war north of the Ohio.

## Kentucky today

Blue Licks Battlefield became a state park in 1927–28, beginning with a 32-acre tract ([Carlisle Mercury, 1928](https://filsonhistorical.org/wp-content/uploads/publicationpdfs/3-1-4_The-Report-on-Blue-Licks-Monument-Dedication-August-1928_Carlisle-Mercury-The.pdf)). A 40-foot granite obelisk was unveiled on August 19, 1928. It lists the Kentucky men by name and quotes both Boone's "enough of honour cannot be paid" and Caldwell's own words ([Carlisle Mercury, 1928](https://filsonhistorical.org/wp-content/uploads/publicationpdfs/3-1-4_The-Report-on-Blue-Licks-Monument-Dedication-August-1928_Carlisle-Mercury-The.pdf)). It names the opposing nations (Shawnee, Delaware, Wyandot and Mingo) but none of their dead ([HMdb](https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=285554)).

Each August the Sons of the American Revolution and the park hold a memorial ceremony at the monument with a color guard ([Lafayette SAR, 2026](https://lexsar.org/event/battle-of-blue-licks-national-event-and-kysssar-state-meeting/)). ⚑ We found no source for a full battle reenactment held every year.

Two Kentucky counties carry the dead commanders' names. [Trigg County](https://history.ky.gov/markers/county-named-1820) (1820) honors Trigg "who gallantly fell…at the battle of the Lower Blue Licks" ([KY Land Office](https://web.sos.ky.gov/land/CountyFormation.aspx/?countyname=Trigg)). [Todd County](https://kentuckygenealogy.org/todd/act_of_legislature.htm) (1819) honors John Todd, great-uncle of [Mary Todd Lincoln](https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/LegislativeMoments/moments09RS/web/Lincoln%20moments%2010.pdf).

The losses of 1782 also fed the push to leave Virginia. In 1784 Benjamin Logan called officers to Danville over frontier defense, because the district "lacked the necessary means and authority" to field its own militia. That meeting began the [ten Danville conventions](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Journals/JSH/1/1/First_Kentucky_Convention*.html) that ended in statehood on June 1, 1792 ([Register of KHS](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Gazetteer/Places/America/United_States/Kentucky/_Texts/RKySHS/44/146/The_Kentucky_Boundary*.html); see [Danville and Constitution Square](/stories/danville-and-constitution-square/)).

## Notes

**Note 1.** Caldwell's report puts his arrival at Bryan's Station on the 15th and the battle on the 18th, one day earlier than the Kentucky accounts (16th and 19th). This article uses the Kentucky dates, which KHS and American Battlefield Trust follow.
**Note 2.** Forces: Filson gives 176, Boone's letter 181 and American Battlefield Trust 182. Caldwell says 300 crossed the Ohio, then "nigh 100" left before the battle; American Battlefield Trust puts about 200 in line; Boone guessed more than 400 from the trail. Losses: Filson gives 67 lost, 7 of them captured; KY National Guard about 64 killed; ExploreKYHistory about 70; Boone 77 killed and 12 wounded. British and Native losses: Caldwell 7 killed and 10 wounded; later accounts about 10–11 killed and 14 wounded.
